Generative AI in the natural & life sciences

What Journals Actually Require

What publishers, journals, funders, preprint servers and research-ethics bodies have actually written down, quoted word for word and re-checked on a schedule — so the answer to “am I allowed to do this?” comes from a source rather than a rumour.

47 organisations1549 quotes, all checked against the stored copy of the page they came fromupdated 2026-11-21

You are probably fine Find what you did What to do What applies The grid Sources Method

Read this first

You have almost certainly not done anything wrong.

Of the 27 publishers and journals assessed here on manuscript writing, none imposes a blanket ban on AI-assisted drafting: 24 allow it under conditions (nearly always with a declaration, and some set stricter rules for particular article types or journals) and 3 ask you to keep AI to language and readability. What every one of the 15 that address it forbids is presenting AI output as your own data. Describe permitted use plainly. A disclosure does not make a prohibited use acceptable.

Where the real lines are

The lines are concrete. Do not list AI as an author. Do not invent citations. Do not present generated content as your data. Do not upload an unpublished manuscript while reviewing it unless the journal explicitly authorizes the tool and use. For language help, follow the journal’s disclosure rule and carry on.

If you write in English as a second language, one more thing

Published policy and screening practice can differ. Across 17 cardiovascular journals studied, 15 used AI-detection software and one said so publicly. You should know that these detectors are unreliable, and unreliable in a specific direction: a widely cited study found they wrongly flagged 61% of essays written by non-native English speakers, against almost none by native speakers. That is a defect in the detectors, not in your writing. It is also why a clear, dated note of what you actually did is worth more to you than to anyone else.

Laffaye TA, et al. Artificial intelligence for manuscript writing: policies and implementation in cardiovascular journals. Cardiovasc Diagn Ther 2025. doi:10.21037/cdt-2025-381 · PMID 41216259

Liang W, et al. GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers. Patterns 2023;4(7):100779. doi:10.1016/j.patter.2023.100779 · PMID 37521038

A policy page, an announcement and a later revision may carry different dates. Springer Nature announced its risk framework on 10 September 2026, although it was already present in the 4 August archive held here. Use the current policy for your decision, and keep a dated copy of the wording you followed.

Springer Nature. Announcement on responsible AI use, 10 September 2026. The framework is also present in the 4 August archive held here. Source

The common cases

Find what you did

"Fixing my English" and "rewriting my text" are not the same thing

Start with what changed. Correcting grammar, tightening phrasing and fixing article use is language editing. Adding arguments, interpretations or conclusions is substantive writing. Translating a draft is a separate activity. Policies draw these boundaries differently; describe the work plainly and use your journal’s rule.

If the distinction is unclear, describe what the tool actually did and check the journal’s rule. A declaration helps readers understand the work, but does not override a prohibition.

Ans M, et al. The Presence and Nature of AI-Use Disclosure Statements in Medical Education Journals. Perspect Med Educ 2026;15:212-225. doi:10.5334/pme.2431 · PMID 41800434

How you word it matters more than you would expect

These say the same thing. The first invites suspicion; the second reads like every other sentence in your methods. Nobody apologises for naming the machine that sequenced their samples, and the tone you write in tells a reader whether you consider this a lapse or a method.

Reads as a confession

The authors admit to having used ChatGPT for assistance with this manuscript and apologise for any errors it may have introduced.

Reads as a method

[Tool and version] was used to [what it did], [when]. All output was checked against the primary sources and revised by the authors, who take full responsibility for the content.

Write it the way you would write any other methods sentence: what, which version, when, and what you did to check it. No apology, no hedging.

Ordered by how often life scientists actually do these things. Verdicts and placement come from the records further down; the advice and the example wording are ours.

Square brackets are yours to fill. Some are plain facts — the tool, its version, the date. Some are your own words, such as which sections were affected. Where you see a slash inside brackets, pick one. If a tool has no version number you can cite, write the name and the date you used it; that is what the date is for.

I used AI to fix my English, or to tidy up my writingdeclare it

Check what the tool changed and what your journal exempts. Some publishers exempt all language editing (PLOS exempts spelling, grammar and rephrasing for clarity or conciseness). Others exempt only basic spelling and grammar checkers and ask you to declare fuller editing. If the model introduced arguments or interpretations, use the drafting guidance below.

PLOS. Ethical Publishing Practice — AI tools and technologies. Checked 20 November 2026. Source

optional wordingyou probably need to write nothing
[Tool and version] was used for language editing only; no content was generated. The authors are responsible for the final text.

Use this optional wording only when it accurately describes the work and your journal does not require a fuller statement.

I used AI to draft or substantially rewrite sectionsdeclare it

Check that your journal permits the kind of drafting you used. Then name the tool, version and sections, and explain your own verification. A declaration describes the work; it does not make a prohibited use acceptable.

example wording
[Tool and version] was used to draft [which sections], accessed [date]. All generated text was verified against the primary sources and substantially revised by the authors, who take full responsibility for the content.

Name the sections. A statement saying only "AI was used in preparing this manuscript" tells a reader little; one study found disclosures averaged 43 words and described the use only superficially.

Ans M, et al. The Presence and Nature of AI-Use Disclosure Statements in Medical Education Journals. Perspect Med Educ 2026;15:212-225. doi:10.5334/pme.2431 · PMID 41800434

I used AI to find papers or build my reference listdeclare it

Check every reference against the original source before you submit: that it exists, says what you claim, and supports the sentence you cite it for. Declare the assistance where your journal asks for it.

example wording
[Tool and version] was used to identify candidate references, accessed [date]. Every reference was subsequently verified against the primary record by the authors.

The second sentence is the one that matters. Say that you checked them.

I wrote in my own language and used AI to translatedeclare it

Check the translation and your target journal’s rule. PLOS recommends disclosure but does not require it; other policies ask for a declaration or specify how the translation should be checked.

PLOS. Ethical Publishing Practice — AI tools and technologies. Checked 20 November 2026. Source

example wording
The manuscript was drafted in [language] and translated into English using [tool and version] on [date]. The translation was checked by [who checked it, and how], and revised by the authors.

If you have no bilingual colleague to ask — and many people do not — say what you did instead. For example, that you translated the English back into your own language and compared it against your original. Describing a real check honestly is worth more than naming a person who did not do one.

I used AI to write, debug or tidy analysis codedeclare it

Report AI assistance with analysis scripts or software code in your methods, including what the tool did and how you checked the result. PLOS explicitly requires disclosure for generating or developing analysis code. This is research-process use; STM’s separate code-presentation category covers formatting code for publication.

PLOS. Ethical Publishing Practice — AI tools and technologies. Checked 20 November 2026. Source

example wording
[Tool and version] was used to assist with writing and debugging analysis code, accessed [date]. All code was reviewed and tested by the authors; analysis scripts are available at [repository].

Report it as software, beside your other tool versions. That is the register it belongs in.

I let an AI agent run analyses, searches or multi-step work for medeclare it

Keep the log: prompts, model and version, dates, tool calls and human checkpoints. A tool name alone cannot explain a multi-step analysis. Follow the journal’s sharing requirements and protect confidential material.

example wording
[Tool and version] was used as an agent to [what it executed: run analyses / search literature / generate and run code], between [dates]. Prompts and session transcripts are provided in [supplementary file]. Human verification was performed at [which checkpoints]; outputs that could not be independently reproduced were excluded. The authors take full responsibility for all reported results.

Keep enough detail to trace the work. Share the records required for review and reproducibility, with sensitive material handled appropriately.

I used AI to make a schematic, diagram or graphical abstractcheck before you do it

Check the image category first. Explanatory diagrams, graphical abstracts, cover art and experimental images have different rules. Where permitted, name the tool and describe its use in the required declaration and caption.

example wording
Figure [n] was generated using [tool and version] on [date] for illustrative purposes; it does not depict experimental data.

Put it in the figure caption, not only in a statement at the end. That is where a reader meets the image. [n] is your figure number.

I used AI to generate or retouch a figure showing my actual datacheck before you do it

A plot made from your data is different from an altered experimental image. Keep the underlying data and reproducible plotting method. Check the journal’s image rules before using AI to retouch a blot, micrograph or scan.

example wording
[Tool and version] was used to produce the plots in Figure [n] from the underlying data, accessed [date]. No image content was added, removed or repositioned; source data are available at [location].

Only use this if it is true. Generating a chart from real data is routine; altering an experimental image is not, and that distinction is where retractions happen.

I used AI while peer-reviewing someone else's manuscriptcheck before you do it

Check the journal’s reviewer policy before using a tool. Science allows revision of your own writing only with tools that do not retain inputs or train on them, and requires disclosure in the review. PLOS allows limited support and requires disclosure available to authors. Permission for writing help does not permit uploading a confidential manuscript.

Science journals. Editorial policies — AI and peer review. Checked 20 November 2026. Source

example wording
In preparing this review I used [tool and version] to [check my own wording / organise my comments], on [date]. No part of the manuscript was entered into any AI tool. All assessments and conclusions are my own.

Describe only what you actually did. Check the tool’s retention and training settings as well as the journal’s confidentiality rules. PLOS requires reviewer disclosures in the review form and editor disclosures in the decision letter, available to authors.

PLOS. Ethical Publishing Practice — AI tools and technologies. Checked 20 November 2026. Source

I am wondering whether generated content can stand in for data I do not havecheck before you do it

No. Every publisher and journal here that addresses this forbids it, and it is the thing all the other rules exist to protect against. If a figure, a value or a participant did not come from your research, it cannot appear as though it did.

There is no wording for this. It is the only outright prohibition STM's classification carries, and no declaration makes it acceptable.

Things this page does not answer

  • Your specific journal. Publisher rules are a starting point. Cell, for example, is stricter than Elsevier on AI cover art. Check the journal instructions as well.
  • Your thesis. University rules apply separately. Check the rules for your programme.
  • Your co-authors. Agree what the declaration says before submission — it describes the whole manuscript.
  • Your funder and preprint server. Their rules apply to different stages of the work. Their records are kept separate from publisher/journal agreement.
  • Cover letters and responses to reviewers. Check the named journal. Permission to edit a response does not authorize uploading a confidential review report.

What to actually do

Keep the record. That is the part you cannot recreate.

Start a log, even a rough one

Model and version, rough dates, the prompts, and the session records themselves. Write the declaration while the work is fresh — a first draft takes ten minutes to write. A transcript from eight months ago cannot be rebuilt, and model versions get retired.

Already required, not hypothetical: ACS, AIP Publishing, Elsevier, Frontiers, JAMA Network, JMIR Publications, MDPI, Royal Society Publishing, Royal Society of Chemistry, The Lancet, Wiley require authors to record or supply tool versions, prompts or session records in some form today.

You already used it and kept no record

Write down what you can still remember — the tool, roughly which version, when, and which parts of the work it touched. Do it now: model versions change and chat histories disappear. Then follow the journal’s disclosure instructions. You do not owe anyone an apology in that sentence.

You already found a fabricated reference in your own draft

Catching a fabricated reference before submission is the system working. Remove or replace it, check every remaining reference against the original source, and carry on. If the error has already been published, contact the journal so the record can be put right.

Save a copy of the policy on the day you follow it

Keep the page, its URL and the date you checked it alongside your research notes. Check it again before submission. A dated copy helps you explain which guidance you followed if the wording changes in between.

Check these before you start

Where a use is prohibited outright, the work cannot be fixed at submission. These are the ones worth checking first, with the publishers and journals here that forbid them:

  • Using AI for illustrative figuresASM Journals, JAMA Network, Science / AAAS
  • Using AI to visualise your research dataACS, ASM Journals
  • Presenting AI output as original dataACS, AIP Publishing, Cell, Elsevier, IOP Publishing, JAMA Network, MDPI, Oxford University Press (OUP journals), PLOS, Royal Society Publishing, Royal Society of Chemistry, Sage, Springer Nature, Taylor & Francis, Wiley
  • Using AI when you peer-reviewJAMA Network

Then check which page applies

Authors, reviewers and editors have different responsibilities. Journal-specific rules can add requirements to a publisher policy. Each record below marks the page and audience to cite.

Where the policies agree

The grid

The evidence grid

Rows follow the nine activities in STM’s 2025 classification, then the ones it leaves out (in italics). Each cell carries two values: whether the use is permitted, and whether it must be declared. silent means we checked and the organisation publishes nothing. — means something weaker: not yet assessed here. Treating those as the same would let unfinished work read as a finding.

A dash means we have not assessed that activity. “Not addressed” means the sources we checked say nothing about it. Neither replaces your journal’s instructions. Start with the rule for what you actually did.

One ACS Publications policy covers authors, editors and peer reviewers. Peer reviewers must not use generative AI to generate, draft or revise their reports, and editors must not hand editorial judgement or decisions to it. Confidential manuscript material may go only into AI tools that ACS has authorised and built into its editorial or peer review systems. AI-generated images cannot be used in Table of Contents graphics.

AIP Publishing's AI policy covers authors, editors and reviewers, and says AI tools cannot be a coauthor. Using AI only to improve readability needs no disclosure, but uses that could affect findings or conclusions must be described in the Methods section. Editors and reviewers may not upload any part of a manuscript or review report into an AI tool that the publisher has not provided or authorised. Authors are advised to check a tool's terms, including how the provider may keep, reuse or redistribute uploaded or generated content; the page does not mention training AI models on authors' content.

For authors, the author section says the journal may request the original images or data during review if there are concerns about their validity, and authors are expected to keep the original files and provide them if requested; these sentences follow the rule on generative AI and original data and images but do not themselves mention AI. Use of AI-generated references that do not exist is called a breach of publication ethics, with no consequence stated. No route of appeal is stated for authors.

AI tools should be used only to improve the language, accessibility or quality of human-generated text, and not for images, cover art, videos or schematics. The Bernoulli Society's AI policy for Bernoulli Journal covers authors, reviewers and editors, and applies to submissions on or after 8 November 2026. Only humans may be listed as authors. Reviewers and editors may share manuscript material only with secure or institutionally approved AI tools whose settings prohibit training on it.

Cambridge sets one general rule for any AI use: it must be declared and explained, authors are accountable for it, and it must not breach Cambridge's plagiarism policy. AI does not meet Cambridge's requirements for authorship, and AI and LLM tools may not be listed as an author. Individual journals may add their own requirements. The policy says: "Please note, individual journals may have more specific requirements or guidelines for upholding this policy."

Cell's journal-policies page requires authors to follow Elsevier's generative AI policy and adds Cell Press rules on explanatory images, data visualisations, research images, cover art and graphical abstracts. AI may not be used to create or alter research or data images, and AI cover art is allowed only as an editorial exception when AI is integral to the research. For peer review, Cell follows Elsevier's policy on generative AI in peer review and points to the Cell Press Information for Reviewers page. See the Elsevier entry for the publisher's own policy.

COPE's position statement says AI tools cannot be listed as an author of a paper, because they cannot take responsibility for the submitted work and, as non-legal entities, cannot assert the presence or absence of conflicts of interest or manage copyright and license agreements. Authors must disclose in the Materials and Methods (or a similar section) how an AI tool was used and which tool, and they are liable for any breach of publication ethics. The statement gives editors no instruction on what to do with a disclosure once received. The page gives 13 February 2023 as its last-reviewed date; its change history lists Version 1 as published on 20 August 2024.

DFG's rules cover reviewers of funding proposals and apply from 16 April 2026. AI may be used only in a supporting role, proposal content may be processed only in systems that guarantee secure and purpose-specific use, and reviewers must disclose AI use. This summary is based on DFG's announcement of 12 March 2026 (Information for Researchers, No. 18); the full Guideline on the Use of Artificial Intelligence in the Review Process is linked from it and has not been read here. The announcement does not mention AI training.

Applies to reviews of funding proposals, from 16 April 2026. AI may be used only in a supporting role. The guideline links such use to four principles (confidentiality, transparency, quality assurance and responsibility). Proposal content may be processed only in systems that guarantee secure and purpose-specific use. All AI-generated content must be critically reviewed. Reviewers must disclose AI use. They will indicate it when submitting the review in the elan portal; the stated purpose is verifiability in the later evaluation and decision-making process. Responsibility for the review stays with the reviewer. elan users must actively consent to observing the guideline when they first log in. elan users must also give a one-off confirmation of a declaration granting the rights needed to use proposal content, including its processing in AI systems in accordance with the guideline.

DOAJ's Guide to applying (Version 2.9) sets out what journal AI policies should include for authors, reviewers and editors. These provisions sit under Best practices, which DOAJ says are not mandatory for indexing, and the guide defines “should” as a recommendation. DOAJ's open access definition lets users pass articles as data to software. The guide does not address licensing content for AI training.

Elsevier's journals policy (updated June 2026) covers authors, reviewers and editors. Reviewers, and editors working outside Elsevier's editorial systems, should use only private AI tools, meaning tools that must not use submitted content to train or improve the AI model. It also tells authors to check an AI tool's terms so that the tool gains only the right to use their material to provide the service, and no right to train on it. The page notes that "the range of AI use varies depending on the journal" but does not say that journals may set their own AI rules. A separate policy for books and commissioned content says authors cannot use output from AI agents or deep research directly as manuscript text, may not upload previously published or copyrighted content into external, open AI tools, and may not use AI to create or alter images (except as part of research design or methods) or to produce covers or graphical abstracts; it also says editors and reviewers should not use generative AI to help evaluate material. The site's copyright notice reserves rights for AI training, but that notice is not part of the AI policy.

The policy page's closing line states 'Policy updated June 2026', while Elsevier Connect announced 'Elsevier has updated its generative AI policies for journals' on 18 August 2026.

The stored copy of the policy page from 1 November 2026 has editors-section wording on private AI tools in Elsevier's editorial systems that the 15 October 2026 copy lacks. Both copies carry the line 'Policy updated June 2026'.

AI tools cannot replace an editor's critical thinking, independent evaluation or final decision-making; editors remain fully responsible for the final decision and its communication to authors. Editors have private AI tools inside Elsevier's editorial systems for tasks such as identifying reviewers, matching scope and detecting duplicate submissions. Outside those systems, editors may use only private AI tools in a supportive capacity and should not upload a submitted manuscript into an AI tool, as this may violate the authors' confidentiality and proprietary rights. The Editors FAQ states without that qualification that editors must not upload submitted manuscripts into AI tools. Elsevier's teams use AI tools at the post-acceptance stage, including proof preparation, copy editing and identifying inconsistencies or inaccuracies in the final paper. The policy does not say that authors are told which tools ran on their manuscript.

Non-binding ERA Forum guidelines for researchers, research organisations and research funders, including AI use in peer review. This fourth version was published on 15 October 2026. Recommendations in non-binding guidelines. Researchers remain ultimately responsible for scientific output. They disclose substantial AI use in research or reporting and describe what it contributed. Researchers also describe how they oversaw and verified AI contributions. When complex tasks are run autonomously, for example with AI agents, researchers set checkpoints so that they validate critical decisions. Using AI agents is never a delegation of control or responsibility. If an agent is given access to sensitive information, the researcher constrains potential confidentiality breaches and remains accountable for how the agent uses that information. Researchers take care not to upload unpublished or sensitive work to an external AI system unless there are assurances that the data will not be re-used. They take care not to provide third parties' personal data to external generative AI systems unless the data subject has given consent and they have a clear goal for its use. For funding proposals, funders are recommended to ask applicants to declare substantial use of generative AI in preparing their application and to describe its role in the research activities proposed and carried out.

Recommendations in non-binding guidelines. They address evaluators, peer reviewers and editors. Peer review remains a fundamentally human process. AI may support it but must not replace the accountability, discernment and professional responsibility of reviewers and editors. AI may be used only for supporting tasks, such as clarifying concepts, background research or language polishing, and only when permitted. The judgement of scientific quality and merit must not be delegated to AI, and AI should not draft evaluation reports. Reviewers and editors remain fully accountable for all assessments, recommendations, judgements and decisions. Unpublished material should not be disclosed through non-secured AI tools or uploaded to AI systems that cannot guarantee confidentiality, data protection and non-use for training. Reviewers use secure, trusted tools, preferably provided by the institution, funder or publisher, and verify factual claims, references and substantive information against original sources. Substantive use, and any other use required by applicable policies, should be disclosed. Where funders allow AI in evaluation, they are to support the allowed uses and help evaluators disclose when and for what purposes AI was used. Funders that give evaluators internal AI tools are to ensure that the tools respect confidentiality and data processing requirements.

Recommendations in non-binding guidelines. Covers editors and research funding organisations. For funders, the material is funding proposals. The guidelines describe no specific publisher or funder AI system. They refer in general terms to funders' internal AI tools and to publisher-sanctioned or institutional tools. Editors do not delegate the judgement of scientific quality and merit to AI, and AI must not replace their accountability, discernment and professional responsibility. AI should not make or substitute for core peer-review judgements, including whether a manuscript should be accepted or rejected. Editors do not disclose unpublished material through non-secured AI tools, and they disclose substantive AI use. Funders remain fully responsible for their own use of generative AI, keep a balance between efficiency, human involvement, supervision and safeguards, and are transparent about that use. Non-delegation of the evaluation of scientific merit must be present throughout the funding process. Funders using AI in internal processes remain aware that applications may contain hidden prompts. Where relevant, they set clear rules prohibiting such manipulation and introduce safeguards. Experimenting with AI demands high levels of transparency with applicants and reviewers while protecting applicants' rights, such as fair treatment, confidentiality and appeal procedures.

Frontiers' AI policy covers authors, editors and reviewers. Authors must disclose AI use in the acknowledgments, and in the methods where applicable, giving the tool's name, version, model and source. Editors and reviewers must not upload manuscript content to external generative AI tools; Frontiers provides its own AI tool for reviewers inside the review forum. The policy page also asks that clinical trials with AI components follow the CONSORT-AI extension and that clinical study protocols with an AI component follow the SPIRIT-AI extension.

The policy page describes two Frontiers AI systems. An internal AI tool in the review forum, operating in a secure, closed environment, summarises manuscript content, highlights areas for analysis and helps reviewers draft feedback; it does not take part in editorial decision-making and should not be used for that purpose. Under the image-manipulation policy, Frontiers’ AI review assistant (AIRA) is trained to detect specific types of recycling, modification and manipulation. Under the heading on AI use by editors and reviewers, manuscript content must not be uploaded to external generative AI tools, to protect confidentiality and intellectual property, and academic editors remain solely responsible for their editorial decisions. The policy does not say whether authors are told that these Frontiers tools were used on their manuscript.

Trigger and consequence: stated for image concerns. Frontiers’ AI review assistant (AIRA) is trained to detect specific types of image recycling, modification and manipulation, and concerns over undeclared image modifications are investigated. Failure to address the concerns leads to rejection, and the issue may be raised with the authors' institutions; after publication, failure to provide the original images may result in retraction. No threshold beyond a raised concern is stated. Author contact: stated; authors are asked to provide the original images and data. Appeal route: the image-manipulation guidance does not refer to one; the general rebuttals and appeals policy lets authors appeal a rejection they believe misapplied a journal policy, considers one appeal or rebuttal per manuscript, and treats all decisions as final. Covers applicants and expert evaluators of Horizon Europe funding proposals. Applicants may use generative AI to prepare a proposal but must disclose which tools they used and how, and remain fully responsible for the content; evaluators must not delegate the evaluation to AI tools. The applicant guidance is in Part B of the application form template (version 5.0, 5 November 2025), and the evaluator rules are in the standard briefing for experts (version 14.0, 15 April 2026). In relevant topics, evaluators also answer whether the project itself uses or develops AI-based systems; that question concerns the funded research.

Applies to expert evaluators of funding proposals. Evaluation must not be delegated to AI tools. AI may be used only for side tasks, such as collecting background information, only where the confidentiality of proposal information and personal data is ensured, and only where evaluators take precautions for the limitations of AI tools, such as hallucinations and biases. Evaluators must document their AI use and make the documentation available to the contracting authority on request. Evaluators remain responsible for keeping proposal information confidential and protecting personal data. Processing proposal information in AI tools that do not respect confidentiality rules, particularly online tools, must be avoided. A breach of confidentiality or personal-data obligations may lead to rejection or reduction of remuneration or costs, or to suspension or termination of the contract.

ICMJE's recommendations have separate pages on AI use by authors, reviewers and editors (Section V, Use of Artificial Intelligence in Publishing). Section II.A.4 says: "Authors should not list AI and AI-assisted technologies as an author or co-author, nor cite AI as an author." Section IV.A on references says: "Referencing AI-generated material as the primary source is not acceptable." The pages give no revision date.

Where this organisation contradicts itself

The reviewer page lets the journal authorise uploading a manuscript to AI where confidentiality cannot be assured ("unless such use of AI is explicitly permitted by journals"). The editor page says the same upload "is prohibited except with authors’ permission". The two pages name different parties who can authorise it.

Dating and tagging oddities

The three Section V pages carry the HTML title tag of Section IV.A: 'ICMJE | Recommendations | Preparing a Manuscript for Submission to a Medical Journal'.

IOP Publishing's generative AI policy covers authors in IOP Publishing-owned journals and in the partner journals listed on the page; other partner journals follow the partners' own ethical policies. Authors must not upload reviewer reports to GenAI tools or use them to generate responses to reviewers, though they may use them to improve the language of their responses; hiding prompts for GenAI tools in a manuscript to manipulate peer review results in immediate rejection. Reviewers are pointed to separate ethical policies for reviewers, which were not reviewed here. A separate text and data mining policy says that, unless a licence or separate written agreement permits it, access to the publications gives no right to build embeddings, vector databases, retrieval or RAG systems or agentic systems from them, and that access through APIs, MCP servers or connectors, automated agents or other machine-to-machine methods needs a separate written agreement.

Trigger and consequence: stated in the AI section. References to non-existent sources are treated as strong evidence of irresponsible AI use. Found during submission, they usually lead to rejection and possibly further sanctions; found after publication, IOP Publishing may retract the paper. Hidden prompts for GenAI tools in a manuscript lead to immediate rejection. Author contact: not stated in the AI section. Under the page's general ethics procedure, possible breaches go to the Research Integrity Team, which contacts the accused individuals for comment before acting. Appeal route: not stated.

A joint initiative of the International Science Council (ISC), COPE, STM and the Global Young Academy (GYA) to develop a global reporting standard for AI disclosure in research, the Vancouver Standard. It is still being developed and is not yet an adopted standard. The second consultation round (July to October 2026) has closed; the third is planned to open in January 2027.

Version 3.0 presents itself as a reference tool that does not prevail over individual publishers' policies. Section 4.2.4.3 lets authors use AIGC tools to structure responses to reviewers unless the journal prohibits it, but forbids uploading the review report, any part of it or identifiable details from it to public AIGC tools. Section 4.1.5 allows AIGC as a language reviewer. A manuscript submitted to public AIGC, or to private services with low data security and confidentiality standards, may become part of a training corpus. Authors should check that the tool's terms do not grant it rights to train on their material, and agree any use for AI training with co-authors and stakeholders in advance. Authors must also ensure the tool imposes no constraints on the use of its outputs that could restrict publication of the article. Section 3.2, on privacy and data security, warns that any content input into AIGC tools may be collected. It advises against submitting sensitive information such as personal identifiers, research participant data or unpublished research materials, and requires authors to comply with the privacy policies, data security protocols and confidentiality requirements of their target publication venue. Section 4.2.3 requires disclosure of AIGC use.

Section 4.1.3 allows AIGC help with choosing chart types and adjusting chart styles. Researchers should ensure that chart adjustments keep the data authentic and accurate. Critical images that present research findings and data must come from the authentic research process and original data, and must not be directly generated or altered with AIGC tools. For deep research tools they verify the reliability of literature databases and review the outputs. Section 4.1.2 allows AIGC help choosing statistical methods and lets researchers use AIGC to interpret data, calculate statistical indicators and perform simple data analysis. Researchers assess AIGC's statistical-analysis suggestions and check them with other reliable tools or subject experts before accepting them. The data used should be collected from the researchers' own experiments or obtained through other legitimate means. AIGC cannot replace the researcher's own interpretation of the data, and researchers verify the results of statistical analysis. Section 4.1.4, on text writing, states that AIGC should not be used to interpret data. Section 4.1.1 asks researchers who use AIGC to collect viewpoint information to monitor and control it and to clean it up if necessary. Section 4.2.1 forbids letting AIGC autonomously initiate, execute or generate research outcomes without direct human supervision and guidance. It adds that AIGC tools cannot be held accountable for published works or research designs, and it stresses the need for human oversight and responsibility throughout the research process. Section 4.2.3 requires disclosure of AIGC use.

Covers authors in JAMA and the JAMA Network specialty journals, published by the American Medical Association. Revised guidance appeared as an editorial on 10 August 2026 (Flanagin, Perlis, Bibbins-Domingo; doi:10.1001/jama.2026.16613) with a table grading fourteen kinds of AI use, and was added to the journals' Instructions for Authors. The table marks AI use in peer review, and for author responses to peer reviewer and editor comments, as not acceptable. The JAMA Instructions for Authors page labels its sections with the journals they include or exclude. The site's copyright notice reserves rights for AI training, but that notice is not part of the AI policy.

The Lancet's Information for Authors (August 2026) gives general AI rules written for authors preparing a manuscript for an Elsevier journal, plus rules for named sections of The Lancet. AI use is not allowed in World Report and Perspectives; in Comments and Correspondence, AI may help only with grammar and spelling, must not be used to translate at submission, and a breach leads to rejection. Other AI use is declared in a separate statement at the end of the manuscript, editors may decide whether the use is appropriate, and AI tools should not be listed or cited as authors. Authors should also check an AI tool's terms so that the tool gets only the right to provide the service to them, with no right to train on their material.

Covers authors, reviewers and Academic Editors. Authors declare all AI use in the cover letter and in an Acknowledgments statement, apart from text editing such as grammar and spelling, and AI tools cannot be listed as authors. Reviewers may use AI only for limited language editing, which they disclose, and Academic Editors must not use generative AI during editorial review or decision-making. Journals decide one point themselves: “The inclusion of AI-generated images for purposes other than data visualization is at the discretion of the journal’s Editorial Board.” Authors must not agree to an AI tool re-using their uploaded material for training unless safeguards for copyright, confidentiality and privacy are in place.

The policy names transparency, reproducibility and accountability as its underlying principles. Use of GenAI tools to assist with preparing manuscripts may be acceptable under some circumstances. All AI tools used must be declared in the cover letter at submission. An Acknowledgements statement should give details of all tools used, describe the prompts and include the product version. The source’s example statement also confirms that the authors reviewed and edited the output. Authors are responsible for the entire content of the manuscript and are fully responsible for its accuracy, validity and integrity, regardless of material contributed by AI tools. Authors must ensure that AI-generated material complies with MDPI’s core and journal-specific editorial policies. MDPI states that some authors use GenAI tools to fabricate entire manuscripts. For narrative and systematic reviews, authors are expected to define the review question, the search strategy and the criteria for selecting included articles. Authors are responsible for ensuring that uploading material to a tool does not breach confidentiality, privacy or copyright, and must not agree to the tool re-using uploaded material for training unless safeguards are in place.

NIH's rules are set out in two Guide notices. Peer reviewers of grant applications and R&D contract proposals, and members of NIH advisory councils and boards, may not use generative AI to analyse or write critiques (NOT-OD-23-149, 23 June 2023). For applications submitted from the 25 September 2025 receipt date, NIH will not treat applications, or sections of them, substantially developed by AI as the applicants' original ideas (NOT-OD-25-132, 17 July 2025). The same notice limits each Principal Investigator to six new, renewal, resubmission or revision applications per calendar year, except for T activity codes and R13 Conference Grant Applications.

openRxiv's approach to AI for bioRxiv and medRxiv, published on 20 October 2026 as eight principles. Authors must be verifiable human beings affiliated with an organisation, and may use AI in drafting and research if they critically review and stand behind the work; the posts set no disclosure requirement. Automated tools support screening, staff make all decisions, and authors can appeal a decline. openRxiv provides a dedicated resource for machine access and text mining and expects all users of its content to respect the authors' chosen licences; the posts do not mention AI training or author consent.

Policy for authors of OUP journals, last updated 13 July 2026 and covering all content types. It sorts AI uses into those permitted without disclosure, those typically permitted with disclosure, and those not permitted. Individual journals can add their own rules. The policy says: "individual journals may have custom requirements, in addition to those stated here, to best serve the needs of their specific research communities." It adds: "In the event of any variation between this policy and the journal’s specific guidance, authors should follow the journal’s specific guidance." Authors confirm at submission that they have followed the policy.

PLOS's policy covers authors, reviewers and editors. Language improvements need no disclosure, disclosure is recommended for translation and required for analysis code and figures, and a cover letter needs none. Editors and reviewers disclose any AI use in the review form or decision letter so that authors can see it, and disclosing AI use does not negatively affect review or editorial decisions. The policy warns that, depending on a tool's terms, data uploaded to it may be ingested into the tool's training dataset.

Policy for all Royal Society journals. All AI use must be disclosed, the published work states which elements were AI-generated, AI must not be listed or cited as an author, and published articles in which AI use is discovered later may be retracted. Journals can ask for more. The policy says: "Journals reserve the right to ask authors who use AI for their corresponding prompts and outputs, which can be supplied as ESM files." Biology Letters announced that from 3 February 2025 it would ask authors who use AI for the tool name, version and date of use in their AI statement, with prompts and outputs as clearly labelled supplementary files.

The RSC sets out its AI rules for authors in three sections of its author responsibilities page: authorship, disclosure and transparency, and image creation and editing. AI tools cannot be listed as an author, and the RSC follows the COPE position statement on AI and authorship. Any generative AI use in preparing the manuscript must be declared in the cover letter at submission; AI-assisted copy editing need not be declared.

Presenting AI output as original dataprohibited, disclosure silent
We do not permit the presentation of any kind of content generated by AI tools as though it were original research data/results from nonmachine sources.rsc.org · Policy page · checked against a saved browser extract
GenAI or AI-assisted tools must not be used to alter images in submitted manuscripts.rsc.org · Policy page · checked against a saved browser extract
Basic adjustments such as brightness, contrast or colour balance are acceptable, provided they do not hide or remove original information.rsc.org · Policy page · checked against a saved browser extract
The only exception is where AI tools form part of the research design or methods, for example, AI-assisted imaging used to generate or interpret research data.rsc.org · Policy page · checked against a saved browser extract
In these cases, authors must describe the process clearly in the Experimental/Materials and Methods section, including how the tool was used, its name, version, and manufacturer.rsc.org · Policy page · checked against a saved browser extract

AI-generated content must not be presented as original research data or results from nonmachine sources. AI tools must not be used to alter images in submitted manuscripts, apart from basic adjustments that do not hide or remove original information. The exception to the image ban is AI that forms part of the research design or methods, such as AI-assisted imaging, which must be described in the Methods.

Using AI to run the research itselfconditional, disclosure required, declared in methods
GenAI or AI-assisted tools must not be used to alter images in submitted manuscripts.rsc.org · Policy page · checked against a saved browser extract
The only exception is where AI tools form part of the research design or methods, for example, AI-assisted imaging used to generate or interpret research data.rsc.org · Policy page · checked against a saved browser extract
In these cases, authors must describe the process clearly in the Experimental/Materials and Methods section, including how the tool was used, its name, version, and manufacturer.rsc.org · Policy page · checked against a saved browser extract
Authors should follow the tool’s usage policies and ensure correct attribution.rsc.org · Policy page · checked against a saved browser extract
Where requested, authors may need to provide original, unaltered images or raw composites for editorial review.rsc.org · Policy page · checked against a saved browser extract

Stated in the image creation and editing section, as the exception to the image-alteration ban. Where AI tools form part of the research design or methods, such as AI-assisted imaging used to generate or interpret research data, authors must describe the process in the Methods, including how the tool was used, its name, version and manufacturer. Authors should follow the tool's usage policies and ensure correct attribution. Original, unaltered images may be requested.

Your submission being screened, including with AI toolspermitted, disclosure silent
We may use image forensics or specialist software to check for irregularities.rsc.org · Policy page · checked against a saved browser extract
If AI usage is suspected and not disclosed, the RSC reserves the right to contact the author for further information.rsc.org · Policy page · checked against a saved browser extract

The RSC may use image forensics or specialist software to check images for irregularities. The AI sections name no AI-text detection tool. If undisclosed AI use is suspected, the RSC may contact the author for further information.

Knowing why you were flagged, and appealingconditional, disclosure silent
If AI usage is suspected and not disclosed, the RSC reserves the right to contact the author for further information.rsc.org · Policy page · checked against a saved browser extract
If concerns are not addressed satisfactorily, the manuscript may be withdrawn, rejected or retracted.rsc.org · Policy page · checked against a saved browser extract

Stated in the AI sections are a trigger, contact with the author and a consequence. If undisclosed AI use is suspected, the RSC may contact the author for further information. If concerns are not addressed satisfactorily, the manuscript may be withdrawn, rejected or retracted. The AI sections state no threshold for suspicion and no route of appeal.

The Methods statement should include the prompts used, and the Acknowledgements should give the tool name and model or version. Where AI forms part of the research design or methods, the Methods must give the tool's name, version and manufacturer, and authors may be asked for original, unaltered images or raw composites for editorial review. The AI sections do not mention keeping session records.

Sage's policy covers authors, reviewers and editors. It sorts AI use into three kinds: assistive (no disclosure needed), generative (disclosure required) and prohibited. It mentions translation only for materials used in the research process and says nothing about translating the manuscript. A separate Sage page says any AI use of Sage content, including training large language models, needs lawful access and a licence from Sage.

AI-produced content that directly impacts the research methodology, analysis, results or conclusions must be disclosed at submission so the editorial team can evaluate it. Authors must verify the accuracy of all outputs and check original sources, because LLMs may generate false content and citations that do not exist. Generation of incorrect text or content is listed as inappropriate use. Generation of a submission using a series of prompts, and plagiarism or inappropriate attribution to prior sources, are also listed as inappropriate use.

Reviewers may use GenAI to help write and format review reports and remain responsible for their content. This sits under the heading for assistive use with no disclosure required. Generating review reports by uploading or pasting the manuscript into a GenAI tool is listed as inappropriate use, and so is use of GenAI tools to conduct peer review. Reviewers who use GenAI tools to generate review reports inappropriately will not be invited to review for the journal, and their review will not be included in the final decision. The journal and publisher reserve the right to take action if reviewers breach peer-review confidentiality by using GenAI tools.

The Science journals' editorial policies cover AI use by authors and reviewers. AI tools cannot be authors, and AI-generated images need explicit permission from the editors. Authors who use AI in the research or as an aid in writing or presenting the manuscript should note this in the cover letter and in the methods or acknowledgments. The page points to separate AI usage guidelines for details by use case; those guidelines are not yet included here, so some activities are not yet assessed.

The Nature Portfolio framework applies to reviewers. Green uses are permitted, and amber uses are permitted with human oversight, verification and disclosure. Green uses are declared by describing the use; amber uses by describing how AI was used and confirming independent judgement. In both cases the reviewer takes accountability for all content in the report. Reviewers must independently verify all outputs and ensure conclusions and recommendations are their own. Generating full review reports, producing accept/reject recommendations, delegating critique to AI and uploading manuscripts to public or unsecured tools are not permitted. Limited use of manuscript content may be acceptable in secure or institutionally approved tools, depending on their data policies.

The presence of an AI declaration does not indicate concern. Editors may seek clarification where a declaration lacks detail, where the declared use appears inconsistent with policy or with the manuscript or report, or where concerns arise regarding accountability, integrity, confidentiality or transparency. Where AI use is not declared, editors may need to investigate or request clarification. Editors intervene where accountability or transparency is unclear, and escalate to their publishing contact where integrity or policy boundaries are breached. The editor guidance says Springer Nature does not expect editors to identify or investigate undisclosed or unsafe uses of AI. Existing integrity, ethics and editorial governance processes apply. Triggers are stated (the conditions above). As a consequence, escalation to a publishing contact is stated; no rejection, correction or retraction for AI use is stated. On author contact, editors may request clarification, but the sources do not say from whom. No appeal route tied to AI concerns is stated.

STM's September 2025 classification defines nine kinds of AI use in manuscript preparation, and this site uses them as its list of activities. It is advisory and leaves policy decisions to publishers; it carries two recommendations over from the 2023 STM Guidelines. Where it is unclear whether a tool counts as AI, it recommends encouraging authors to declare the tools they used and how. It also recommends that publishers state the level of disclosure they require, such as particular tools or the exact prompts used with generative AI tools.

Individual journals genuinely differ from this policy — check your specific journal as well.

The policy says individual journals may restrict AI use further: "Note that some journals may not allow use of Generative AI tools beyond language improvement, therefore authors are advised to review the “Instructions for authors” on the journal homepage prior to submission." Book authors must ask their editorial contacts to approve any planned AI use, at the proposal stage or during writing; an approved statement goes in the preface or introduction of the book. The policy warns that generative AI providers may reuse input or output data, for example for AI training.

Policy on generative AI in the application and assessment process for all UKRI funding opportunities. It covers applicants, assessors (reviewers and panellists) and UKRI's responsibilities as a funder. Applicants must not use generative AI during interviews that form part of the application process. Upheld allegations of misconduct arising from generative AI use can lead to sanctions, including rejection of applications and termination of funding.

WAME's recommendations (revised 31 May 2023) are meant to inform editors and help them develop journal policies, and to help authors and reviewers attribute chatbot use. Chatbots cannot be authors. Chatbot help with drafting is noted in the acknowledgment; research uses are stated in the Abstract and Methods. WAME warns that chatbots keep the content and prompts supplied to them and may use them in future responses.

Individual journals genuinely differ from this policy — check your specific journal as well.

Wiley's AI guidelines cover research-process use, agentic search and disclosure; AI tools must not be listed as authors. The ethics guidelines leave the decision to each journal: "The final decision on whether using AI Technology is appropriate or permissible for a submitted manuscript or a published article belongs to the journal’s editor or other party responsible for the publication’s editorial policy." The AI guidelines add: "Check the specific requirements of your target journal, as policies vary across publishers and titles". Authors must make sure an AI tool's provider gains no rights over their content, including the right to train on it, and should check the tool's terms for clauses on ownership, data reuse, training or opt-out.

The journal’s editor, or another party responsible for the publication’s editorial policy, decides whether AI use is appropriate.

Method

What this does and does not claim

Word for word, or not at all

Every verdict carries a short quote, its source, and how it was obtained. All 1549 quotes are checked automatically against the stored copy of the page they came from; the build fails if any quote cannot be found. An earlier version of this site carried a sentence in quotation marks that turned out to be a research assistant’s paraphrase. That is what this check exists to prevent.

47 of 69 sources are fetched directly. 5 retain dated Internet Archive captures; their current pages are checked separately and carry a live-check date. 17 use a saved excerpt from the rendered browser page, labelled as such. A fixed archive capture does not establish that the live policy is unchanged. Missing live checks enter the monitoring queue.

Published policy only

This records what organisations have published. It cannot see what editors actually do. Across seventeen cardiovascular journals studied, fifteen ran AI-detection software and one said so publicly — the gap between stated and practised is real, and this site does not close it.

47 organisations are recorded here, activity by activity. If your journal, funder or institution has no entry, it has not been assessed; that says nothing about whether it is silent. 1 substantive internal contradiction and 5 dating or tagging oddities are recorded across them. A stale HTML title tag is not a policy contradiction and is not counted as one, and differences in audience or product scope are kept separate. Where we could not find wording at all, the activity stays unassessed and is never labelled silent.

Corrections and right of reply

If you work for an organisation recorded here and think a record is wrong, we want to fix it. Every record names its source and quotes the wording it relies on, so corrections can be specific. Open an issue and we will respond. Corrected records carry the date they changed, and the change stays in the public history.

This page declares itself unmaintained automatically once its oldest record passes 550 days without re-checking. The closest precedent to this project still serves a live page, with no staleness warning, four years after its last update.
